This week, the United States Department of Commerce issued a rule that blocks Chinese AI firms "and other restricted entities from remotely accessing America’s advanced AI chips." This, after a week that saw the ousting of ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been asked to testify before Congress to address "clear national security concerns".

John Moolenaar, the head of the US Select Committee on China, took to X to say the following

This rule sends a message to the CCP that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years. Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy. This new rule is an important step in keeping chips out of ill-intentioned hands, strengthens our national security laws, and will help protect America's lead in the AI race

The exporting of top-of-the-line American AI chips to China is banned, but if Chinese firms can get remote access, they can still train AI models even without physically handling the hardware. Effectively, getting remote access means being able to use the chips' compute without being physically there.

America has been very hot and cold with how it wants China to approach AI. It has banned leading AI chips, but allowed somewhat nerfed ones into the country, only to say in an earnings call this week that Nvidia wouldn't be shipping more "Hopper data centre products". And China, too, has gone back and forth on how many American-made AI chips it will take.

Today, @CommerceGov issued a rule to block Chinese AI firms and other restricted entities from remotely accessing America’s advanced AI chips. Chairman @RepMoolenaar praised the decision in the following statement: pic.twitter.com/SrIDbAWZPYNovember 16, 2026

Earlier this year, Trump, alongside Elon Musk, Tim Cook, and Jensen Huang, flew to Beijing in the hopes of opening up China to AI trade. Effectively, America wants to sell enough AI chips to China to make a profit from it, but not so much—or at lest not so many advanced chips—that it loses its edge in the worldwide AI arms race.

Being able to remotely access chips skips the income the US would get from selling them, and would give Chinese firms access to the top-of-the-line models, theoretically giving it the computational power to catch up to America.

All of this makes some sense from the perspective of those gunning for the US to be at the forefront of the AI race, but it does make one wonder why it took so long for such a rule to take effect. The AI race has been ongoing for years now. The China-based DeepSeek open-source model caused a ruckus early last year, as it demonstrated just how quickly Chinese AI had developed.

#3784. Worst Class Ever takes asymmetrical multiplayer back to school, with a teacher player trying to spot the naughty children among the NPCs

Master the sinful art of eating sweets behind your textbook

What's the best prank you ever pulled on a teacher in school, assuming you went to school? By which I mean, a genuinely funny prank that didn't cause any injuries, break any of the more important laws (legal or ethical), or leave anybody with years of mental distress.

I'll start: I once had to write a four-page punishment essay with the topic "silence is golden", after being caught talking in class. I took the essay very seriously for the first three pages, only to end it with the phrase "...but not as golden as my arse." The teacher who set me the essay smugly tore it up without reading it - as I knew he would. Checkmate, Mr Thompson. Decades later, the last laugh remains mine.

Worst Class Ever is a new don't-call-it-friendslop asymmetrical multiplayer game dedicated to such larks. One player is a teacher, and seven others are naughty delinquent children, hiding in amongst some well-brought-up and obedient NPCs. As the wayward tykes, your goal is to do mischievous things like eating at your desk, passing notes, dropping banana skins, and playing on your phone, without being spotted by Teach.

All of this takes place in a breezy modern Japanese high school, the kind familiar from a million animes. Bagsy the Protagonist Desk by the window at the back of the class! The maplist spans the curriculum, from computer labs to gym tracks to stepped lecture theatres. I don't think there are any covert edu-tainment mechanics, but if you're playing Teacher, I guess there's nothing to stop you actually explaining the periodic table while trying to work out who keeps throwing chalk at your head.

What a wholesome and whimsical place! Such happy memories! Oh crikey, the male teacher is terrifying – why can't he stop grinning? And why do I have a smoke grenade? Why is this lesson taking place in the dark? Why are the teachers permitted to punch the students and tie them to wooden posts? Worst Class Ever definitely isn't a horror game, but I'm not sure I'd send my kids to this particular institution. I feel like we're one texture pack away from playing a more sociable version of Little Nightmares. Read more on Steam.

#3783. The Blood of Dawnwalker is getting a New Game Plus mode in next week's update

UPDATE 17TH NOVEMBER: The Blood of Dawnwalker update 1.2 - the update that brings a New Game Plus mode, predominantly - is now available on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S/X.

New Game Plus, as mentioned below, raises the level cap to 100, and scales enemies and regions in the game around you. Previously, the game was zone-scaled, so some zones were tougher than others. In New Game Plus, this will no longer be the case, so you can go and explore Xanthe's region at the back of Vale Sangora straight away, if you want to.

There'll be new versions of equipment with new stats to find, and they'll be labelled with "NG+" so you know when you've picked one up. You can unlock New Game Plus from the main menu after choosing your base save and difficulty option. All of your accrued skill perks and abilities will be available to you at the start of the Withering Away quest in the game's prologue.

The full patch notes for Dawnwalker update 1.2 are:

ORIGINAL STORY 13TH NOVEMBER: A New Game Plus mode is coming to vampiric RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker next week.

Developer Rebel Wolves has now detailed everything coming with The Blood of Dawnwalker's Update 1.2, currently planned to go live sometime next week, and top of the list of changes is a New Game Plus for players who have already rolled credits on the game.

"If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with New Game+," the developer revealed earlier today. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over." Rebel Wolves is upping the level cap to 100 for New Game Plus, which will also have items with updated stats and enemies "balanced and scaled uniformly across all regions."

Elsewhere in Update 1.2, the studio is making tweaks to "enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat," and improving terrain geometry to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration." We'll need to wait for more comprehensive patch notes before finding out which enemies are getting spongier or flimsier, however.

While the incoming patch doesn't seem to be as beefy as the last - the one that added animal petting and an easier Story mode - it'll be a good way to sink your teeth deeper into a game that's already begging to be replayed, thanks to a time management mechanic that can drastically change any given run.

The new game from some former The Witcher 3 veterans came out in September and seems to have been a hit. Eurogamer's The Blood of Dawnwalker review called the game a "familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful."

If you own a pair of headphones in GTA 6, you can even listen to your favorite shows while on foot for the very first time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar has made some vital changes to the way that you listen to music, access podcasts, and change radio stations in GTA 6. You can even listen to music outside of your vehicles for the first time, so long as you have the necessary headgear purchased and equipped.

Below you'll find a quick rundown of how to listen to music in GTA 6, how to access on-demand podcasts, and where to buy your own headphones to listen to your favorite songs from the GTA 6 soundtrack while you're roaming around the world of Leonida.

There are radios in GTA 6 everywhere. In your safehouse, in whatever vehicles you're driving around, and sometimes you'll find them out in the world too. Thankfully, how to use a radio and change stations in GTA 6 rarely changes.

When you're driving a car you'll want to hold Left on the D-pad to access the radio controls. This is also true for radios in the world, bikes, boats, and planes. Whilst you are holding Left on the D-Pad, you can scroll between all of the radio stations either with L1/LB and R1/RB, or with the right thumbstick. Select the station that you want, stop holding the D-pad button, and it'll start playing. You can also go into this menu and press X/A to turn off the radio entirely.

You can also activate 'On Demand' programming in GTA 6 like podcasts in a similar way. Activate that radio menu again by holding Left on the D-pad, only now you want to press Down with the right thumbstick. This will let you access all of the podcasts which are available to you. You can even press Square/ X on each to scroll between episodes, and then press X/A to play.

Tip: If you actively go into the on-demand section of the radio menu, you can pause the podcast that you're listening to. Head back in here later (regardless of whether you're on foot or back in a vehicle) and it'll sync playback up to where you left off.

Buying a set of headphones allows you to listen to radio and podcasts while outside of a vehicle. To get headphones, open the GTA 6 Index and scroll to the Style tab. In here you're looking for the 'Electronics' option which will display all shops that sell these items, ordered by the one that's closest to your current location. Head over to one of these stores to purchase a pair of headphones or earbuds – these range upwards of $100 for a basic set through to more luxurious models depending on the store, and remember that both Jason and Lucia will need to purchase their own.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Once you have purchased headphones in GTA 6, you'll need to equip them. Hold L1/LB to open your loadout and press R1/RB to navigate to the items tab. The second slot in the wheel is for headgear; navigate to this slot with the right thumbstick and press X to equip your headphones. From there, it's as easy as holding Left on the D-pad to access the radio stations and on-demand podcasts.

If you bought headphones and now can't find them in the menu, it's possible that you have lost them in combat. If you get attacked by the cops or a civilian in the world with headphones equipped, these can get knocked to the ground. Don't forget to pick them back up once you're done brawling, otherwise they will be lost forever!

#3780. While soulslikes went bigger than big, Death's Door swung open the appeal of a tighter adventure

Declaring a Best Way of Doing Things is a fool’s game, though in recent years my favourite entries in the Tricky Hitting genre – inclusive of soulslikes and their hybridised disciples – have been the big, bulging ones. Elden Rings and Silksongs, with vast kingdoms and deep, rattling toolkits for surviving them. The reason it’s a fool’s game is because you can also have something like Death’s Door, a taut, compact, lighthearted little actioner that fills eight hours instead of 80 and yet never feels underwhelming or compromised for it.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Even in the latter stages, with a full kit of precisely four ranged spells, Death’s Door is a simple proposition. You are a crow. You hit things. Occasionally you shoot things. You collect the souls of a frog, a yeti, and a grandmother. Everything in-between directly relates to finding the errant monster/pensioner, or at a stretch, upgrading one of those four abilities.

Still, it’s clever with its limitations. Environments are small in number but vary wildly in tone and texture, and they tightly weave their paths into criss-crossing bundles that maximise travel – evoking the sense of a great, ranging adventure within relatively tiny spaces. The lack of a wiki’s worth of combat options also never becomes a problem, partly because it spreads out its spell unlocks, and partly because the smooth, flowing back-and-forths of its central swordplay are pleasurable enough to carry it anyway. Good bosses, too! They’re all characterful, memorable weirdoes who fight unlike anyone in their minion armies, and usually come with a hidden weakness to deduce and exploit.

Which is welcome, as these big lads and lasses do tend to launch difficulty spikes right up your feathered backside, and do so in a game that isn’t otherwise as fussed about trial-and-error pain endurance as some of its inspirations. They don’t, however, bring the mood down. At times, this tale of a pitch-black soul reaper working as an agent of Death (complete with an office of Death and embittered co-workers of Death) can get downright cosy, leading through you through warmly-lit jungles and breezy waterside ruins.

Recently replaying, I’d also forgotten how witty it can be. Little gaglets are sprinkled throughout, both visual and verbal, but the best jokes are saved for – funnily enough – the bosses, who’ll raise your pre-fight spirit with some amusingly terrible trash talk before becoming the punchline themselves. I audibly wheezed the first time a death animation immediately cut to the foe’s impromptu funeral, their beaked killer among the precious few guests. And even when the joke is recycled later, I couldn’t help tittering at the sight of my enemy – who seconds earlier, had been attempting to fatally sit on me – lying nobly in state.

I previously considered ending my Valor Mortis review by calling it a gateway into the more demanding side of action-RPGs; a shorter, simpler alternative to FromSoft’s overwhelming titans that might nonetheless serve to introduce curious newcomers to their shared quirks and qualities. The game equivalent of splashing your chest with water before jumping into a pool. In hindsight, Death’s Door was always a better fit for that description, though there’s enough else here you don’t need to be prepping for something tougher to appreciate its lean, keen adventuring.

#3779. Magic: The Gathering animated series Planeswalker is coming to Netflix in 2027

Netflix's long-gestating Magic: The Gathering animated series is called Planeswalker, and it's coming in 2027.

The title was revealed at MagicCon Atlanta, and Netflix shared a first look at the show on Twitter/X on 13th November. "Every great story begins with a spark. Here's your first look at Planeswalker, a new animated series based on Magic: The Gathering. Coming to Netflix in 2027", the company wrote, and shared a teaser, which you can see below:

According to a synopsis shared with IGN, the series follows Chandra Nalaar, "a volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past". It continues: "Confronted by an insidious force, Chandra and some of the most legendary Planeswalkers must harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence".

Netflix first announced a Magic: The Gathering series in June 2019, with Avengers: Endgame directors Joe and Anthony Russo attached, and it was originally due in late 2022. Two years in, the original showrunners departed over creative differences, and in September 2024, Netflix confirmed it had started again from scratch with Star Trek: Picard and 12 Monkeys showrunner Terry Matalas in charge.

IGN reports that Matalas, who most recently ran Marvel's VisionQuest, is running the show alongside Cindy Appel. Budapest-based studio DIGIC Pictures is handling the animation.

At the end of last month, we learned PUBG is also being turned into a live-action series for Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct, write, executive produce, and star.

As I write this, reviews for Grand Theft Auto 6 have gone live. Gamers in New Zealand have been able to play it for almost six hours, and millions of people farther west are eagerly waiting for clocks to hit midnight in their own timezones. In preorder sales alone, GTA 6 has already generated over $1.6 billion in revenue, and will undoubtedly earn millions more over its launch weekend.

As Rockstar is poised to set historic records with its latest release, the workers who made it could be making history of its own: Over 1,600 Rockstar employees in the UK are currently voting on whether to form a union. If it wins recognition when the ballot closes on November 26, the Rockstar Games Workers Union would be the largest in the UK games sector, organizing workers at what's arguably the games industry's highest-profile studio—a major milestone in the push for unionization in game development.

In an op-ed for The Guardian, Rockstar animation programmer and union representative Nestor Uriarte said the studio's possible unionization is the product of a decade-long realization that "to tackle the industry's mounting challenges we need to come together." Union recognition, he said, would help safeguard the working conditions of the developers who built GTA 6 into an already record-breaking success.

"Behind these numbers are thousands of people whose talent and hard work make the games possible. With a recognized union, we can ensure everyone, across every department, sees a fair share of the success we contributed to," Uriarte said. "Our games are industry-leading. Our wages, conditions and bonuses should be too."

Working conditions at Rockstar produced one of the early flashpoints in the advancing push for games industry unionization over recent years, sparked by employees' descriptions of its "death march" crunch culture and allegations of sexual assault. While the studio's taken steps towards a healthier workplace in the years since, employees have reported continuing concerns around gender pay gaps, crunch, and nebulous bonuses conditions.

Coinciding with the union vote, a Glasgow tribunal is weighing testimonies in the ongoing legal battle around Rockstar's alleged union-busting and firing of employees who had been involved in organization. Meanwhile, just days before a launch that's projected to earn landmark revenue, Rockstar parent company 2K reportedly laid off a third of the employees at XCOM and Civilization developer Firaxis.

"It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off," Uriarte said. "But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Union recognition, he said, would also provide developers with a greater ability to negotiate the rapid proliferation of AI in game development, which represents yet another threat of worker devaluation in an industry where one third of the labor force has been laid off in the last two years. A Rockstar union would help protect its workers' future—and the future of the studio.

"We’ve heard from colleagues who are nervous that the union is an outside troublemaking force that will threaten the company," Uriarte said. "But we’re not outsiders. We are hundreds of studio employees who live for Rockstar, its output, and the players. We want to see it succeed."

#3776. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is getting three big updates with new starting scenarios - organ trading, junk empires and fine dining

Mucky and disreputable kiosk game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim is getting three big updates over the next few months that add extra starting scenarios, building on the existing wealth of goods, materials, vocations and techs. Those starting scenarios range from peddling human meat to running the finest cyber-frappucino stall this side of Tannhäuser Gate. There are no hard release dates, and the contents of each update may alter, but developers Questing Goose Studio have shared some rough timeframes.

Coming up in mid-December, there's the Junker starting scenario, which I assume is all about trading scrap, rather than being a Prussian nobleman. You'll get a bespoke perk, new items, and the ability to hire, equip and send scavs on expeditions. This update will also include some minor expansions for the Fence and Gunsmith vocations – the latter will be able to flog or otherwise make use of shotgun shells, 25mm grenade rounds and a tier 3 handmade SMG, alongside new armour.

Late January is when you'll "very likely" get the chance to be an Organ Dealer, care of the second major update. "Players will start by buying different organs and fulfilling specific requests, and will later be able to grow or print organs," a Steam blog explains. You'll also be able to filter blood and remove diseases, with different blood types having different value modifiers. How will you get your hands on organs? By sending horrible black market thugs on foraging "expeditions".

Last but not least, the planned April update will add the Street Food Vendor starting scenario. This lets you weave a livelihood around choice beverages and edibles from a range of cultures, supported by updates to the game's Aquaculture and Hydroponics tech. Sounds a lot cheerier than the organ trading racket, but then again, Probably Stolen will doubtless find a way to make it utterly grim. Guests at Sweeney's Cantina know better than to ask what our frappucinos are made of.

Are you playing Probably Stolen? It's been doing better than expected. I was keen on the demo, but my attention was lured away by a truly upsetting game about dogpeople in caves.

#3775. Call of Duty Endowment marks Remembrance Day with veterans' Valor Pack push

The Call of Duty Endowment is marking Remembrance Day and its 17th anniversary by encouraging Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone players to pick up its Valor Pack, with all of Activision's net proceeds going towards helping veterans find jobs.

The Call of Duty Endowment Valor Pack - which has been available since Modern Warfare 4 launched on 23rd October - was designed by the Endowment and Infinity Ward with US Marine Corps veteran and Medal of Honor recipient Kyle Carpenter in mind.

The items include a melee weapon blueprint inscribed with "Worth Fighting For", plus items called Relentless and Still Standing.

According to the Call of Duty blog, 100 percent of Activision's net proceeds from the pack (after VAT and sales tax) go to the Endowment.

To mark Remembrance Day, players who owned it and launched either game before 6pm GMT on 12th November also received double XP tokens and a DMZ survival kit.

"Veterans bring incredible skills into the workplace after military service," said Carpenter.

The Endowment, which supports veterans in the UK as well as the US, says it has now helped place more than 180,000 into "high-quality jobs", and wants to reach 200,000 by 2030.

Other partners are also raising money, with Pilot's round-up campaign raising more than £4.7 million ($6 million) for the Endowment since 2019. Polaris will also donate around £19,500 ($25,000) if players collectively complete 5 million rides in its DAGOR vehicle across Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone by 25th November.

It comes two weeks after Activision apologised to bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it would remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Players discovered that the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died.

The Wanted Level goes up to six now, but it isn't for the faint of heart

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the entirety of my time playing the game for review, I was only able to reach a six-star Wanted level in GTA 6 the one time. That's partially because I was hell bent on maintaining a 'Professional' Criminal Profile in GTA 6, and also because it's really difficult to activate. You have to really be on a bit of a mad one to get this level of heat coming down on you.

If you aren't aware, GTA 6 brought back six stars to the Wanted system. You typically gain heat for doing everything from trespassing to petty crime to big bank robberies, with different numbers of stars indicating the volume of cops (and eventually military) who respond to try and bring you in.

My only six-star encounter in GTA 6 was the result of a firefight with a regular citizen that went awry, the accidental throwing of a grenade at a bunch of cop cars, and then a high-speed pursuit which lasted for well-over 15 minutes and eventually resulted in me hijacking an aeroplane in a desperate attempt to gain some ground. As it turns out, it's only mass destruction and loss of life which will get you six-stars of trouble in GTA 6.

The problem with getting a 6-star wanted level in GTA 6 is that there's actually no way to resolve it. Once you've got that sort of heat on you, the cops and the military will not stop in their pursuit of you. My poor aeroplane lasted just minutes after jets were dispatched to bring me crashing down to Earth.

Interestingly enough, there is a GTA 6 cheat code to raise the wanted level, but no matter how many times I put in the activation code, it would never go above five stars. Which is all to say, the game really is only giving you a 6 star wanted level in GTA 6 when you really deserve it. And then once you've got it… settle in for some pretty outrageous carnage.

#3773. What are we all playing this weekend?

Ah, yes, Saturday. Traditionally a day for relaxing. Why is it then I'm packing, doing last-minute shopping, and going to a wedding all in the space of eight hours? Because, Julian, you are a fool who, as ever, has left everything far too late.

What about the team, though. I imagine they've managed their time much better.

JamesI've got a date with Derelikt, a retro survival-horror FPS with just a dash of immsim keycode hunting. I'm not expecting gee-oh-tee-why material but I do respect any game whose minimum system requirements read, in their entirety, "Sound Card: Toaster Spec".

MarkLast weekend of freedom before I, both cheekily and I assure you temporarily, abandon my PC in order to play a certain game I've been waiting for since I was about 14. I should probably play something strategy-oriented or with extra swanky graphics to get in some more preemptive atonement for my sins. I might end up playing Sleeping Dogs instead.

OllieI want to spend more time in Marathon this weekend. The PvE roguelite-ness of Cryo Archive is intriguing, and I want to see how different the runs can get.

EdwinThis weekend I'm going to shop for a fan heater. I have an unhealthy love of fan heaters. They are my spirit animals. I fancy upgrading to one of those big Dyson things that looks like a mini hyperspace jumpgate, but I assume they're costly both to buy and run.

CallumWith GTA 6 now looming on the horizon, I shall spend this weekend with as few video games as possible. I’ll sit and meditate, like a great warrior prepping for the war to come. Many guides shall be written. Many hours shall be spent looking at virtual guns. Many digital policemen's lives will be taken with big bazookas. But for now, I rest… and probably eat a lot of food.

JeremyThis is the last weekend I must work on our Castlevania walkthrough after almost 50 days of continuous effort. The end is in sight and only then will the morning sun come to vanquish this horrible night.

JulianWhy have I still got too much to do? Because for some reason I decided to start a new BattleTech campaign this week and didn't use my evenings productively crossing items off my to-do list. If I get a free hour (ha!) I'll settling into my mech and cause a ruckus.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

#3772. Ubisoft is reportedly making a new Rainbow Six Vegas game, nearly two decades after Vegas 2

Ubisoft is reportedly working on a new Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

According to Insider Gaming, the project is in early development at Ubisoft Montreal under the codename Spades. It’s one of three new projects reportedly in production at the studio, and sources suggest a second of those is also set in the Rainbow Six universe. Eurogamer hasn’t been able to verify the report.

It’s not yet clear what form the new game will take, but Insider Gaming’s sources said it's "likely Vegas 3 rather than a remake" of an existing game. Insider Gaming expects it will be several years before Ubisoft officially announces a new Vegas game.

Rainbow Six Vegas launched in 2006, followed by Rainbow Six Vegas 2 in 2008. Since then, the series has centred on 2015's Rainbow Six Siege, and in August, Ubisoft announced Rainbow Six Tactics, a single-player, turn-based spin-off from Ubisoft Paris due in 2027.

Rainbow Six now sits under Vantage Studios, the Ubisoft subsidiary set up last year that also oversees Assassin’s Creed and Far Cry, and in which Tencent holds a 26.32 percent stake.

Last week, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on two new Assassin's Creed games: one set in ancient Rome, and a mobile spin-off set in Jerusalem. The leak came less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

You will have to wait till next year to mess with your Large Knob.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

So you may or may not have heard this, but Wooting has a Large Knob coming out soon. Think a traditional keyboard volume dial, but, yeah, large. And also available by itself without a keyboard. Well, Wooting opened up preorders for its $40/£34 Lekker Knob Large this year and the 80HE+, which was expected to launch in 2026, has now been pushed back to 2027. Big news, I know.

In a video titled "We found an issue with the Large Knob…", Wooting co-founder and CEO Calder Limmen announced that the Large Knob has been delayed by at most four months (it has moved back to March, 2027).

Limmen says he wanted to ship in December but "at the same time, I also had to make a decision and delay the Large Knob so that we don't ship a Large Knob with issues".

Limmen says 30% of the Large Knobs have a defect and they don't know why. They reportedly had a torque issue where larger production batches couldn't get the same level of resistance from each knob, which was then fixed by mounting the ball bearing inside the knob differently and changing some internals. But then, with the new batch, using a temperature chamber for testing, they spotted inaccurate testing in 30% of devices.

Effectively, the representation of the wheel in the software and the wheel itself had different values. If you simply have to swivel the wheel to use it, that wouldn't be a problem, but the Large Knob reportedly uses very specific movements in its software, so it needs absolute clarity over where exactly the dial is pointing.

That all means the next few months will involve Wooting engineers looking inside the Large Knob, performing more temperature tests and trying to figure out why this defect is happening.

Limmen also clarifies that if they figure out the problem much sooner, they will ship it earlier than January. The March 2027 release date is effectively a worst-case scenario.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

As for those who have ordered the Large Knob, Wooting are handling the delays in different ways depending on how you ordered. If you picked up the Large Knob alongside a keyboard (other than the 80HE+, which comes with the knob built in), Wooting will ship the knob and keyboard separately, paying for the shipping. If you bought the keyboard with the built-in knob, it has also been delayed to March 2027, but will come with the travel case for free now.

If you bought the Large Knob by itself, you will get "some goodies [added] to your order." It's not clear yet what those goodies are, but a few extra is a nice way to make up for a delay.

#3770. The First Zombie launches December 16

The First Zombie, the “reverse” zombie game produced by Kentaro Fujii of Japanese variety show Wednesday’s Downtown, will launch for Switch and PC via Steam on December 16, Phoenixx announced. It will support English and Japanese language options.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

Play as humanity’s very first zombie! In this unique zombie game, you don’t kill the undead—you multiply them. “Make friends” with humans to grow your horde and transform Tokyo into a city of zombies!

A “Reverse” Zombie Game Where Zombies Save the World

Produced by Kentaro Fujii (Wednesday’s Downtown)!

A zombie game where the protagonist is humanity’s very first zombie!? With a mission to “lead humanity to a brand-new stage,” the one who has arrived on the streets of Tokyo is…

In this game, your objective isn’t to defeat zombies, but to increase their numbers. Approach the humans just going about their daily lives, “make friends” with them, and turn them into zombies. Grow your undead horde and flood the city streets with your new companions!

The Stage is Tokyo. Turn It Into a City of the Undead.

Shibuya, Shinjuku, Ueno… Conquer each district with your horde and transform them into zombie towns!

#3769. Missed something on your first go around The Blood of Dawnwalker? I've got good news, as next week's update adds in new game plus

A big part of the point of The Blood of Dawnwalker is that you're on a fixed time limit. You've got 30 in-game days and nights to try and save your family, and if you don't manage to see everything the game has to offer, well, the game's director is fine with that. But that doesn't matter as much now, as The Blood of Dawnwalker is getting its 1.2 update next week that adds in a new game plus mode.

"If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with New Game+!" a post from the devs explains. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over; the level cap will be raised to 100; enemies will be balanced and scale uniformly across all regions; and items will have NG+ versions with updated stats." Sounds like your usual new game plus affair! I suppose it is a good opportunity to try out different things compared to your first playthrough, but I'm not exactly aligned with the idea that the timer restriction is too restricting (as some mods have made clear how others feel that way).

In any case, the update goes a tad further than that. If you got the Eclipse Edition of the game, the in-game soundtrack that came with it "will be extended with additional songs from the game." You can expect the soundtrack on streaming services soon, too. While details are slimmer here, there are also some planned balance changes, like updated enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat, and terrain geometry has seen some improvements to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration."

Overall, a bit of a smaller update compared to the last one, but one I'm sure will be welcome to some all the same. If you've not had a chance to check the game out yet and still feel on the fence about it, here's some lovely words from Mark's review: "There’s always that sense that something important or unexpected could be lurking around the next corner, to pull you into a quest dripping with depth and intrigue. It works to ensure the more busywork-esque tasks attached to angering Brencis and his Boyars never make Vale Sangora feel home to a string of boring boxes to tick. It’s a vibrant, constantly changing place with a thousand different threads metaphorically criss-crossing just beneath its surface, just as ancient ruins literally criss-cross beneath its swamps, crags, and forests."

#3768. The latest GTA 6 leak comes in the form of a 34-song tracklist for GTA 6: The Album, featuring Dua Lipa, Lana Del Rey, Rina Sawayama, and more

We are now just four days away from the release of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X/S and PS5, but the proximity to the much-anticipated launch date isn't stemming the tide of leaks that has been plaguing the game for much of the past year. Yesterday, a new video - seemingly from a record store that received vinyl records of the soundtrack early - showed off the full 34-song tracklist for the game.

Thanks to the listing printed on the back of Grand Theft Auto 6: The Album vinyl, we have a better idea of the licensed music that'll appear in-game. Travis Scott, Rina Sawayama, Cardi B, Pinkpantheress, SZA, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Jennie, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson are just some of the names that make up the impressive list. We know about a few of these tracks from September's announcement of the record, but only six tracks were revealed then, not the whole list.

Take a look at the full track listing below:

You can expect to hear these tracks on the radio - alongside many more, no doubt - and deployed at curated times during cutscenes or in missions, to really tie together the vibe of the city. This is something Vice City did remarkably well its roster of 80s tracks, and I can't wait to see how Rockstar has used more contemporary music in the same way here.

Of course, there have been a lot of Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks in the run-up to the game's launch. Another recent example is the full game's map which seemingly leaked online thanks to the £350 collector's edition on show in a UK department store. Then there were all the leaks from a group calling itself CyberLeek, which shared unofficial gameplay and map details over the course of a few weeks, before Rockstar had even revealed much gameplay itself.

Amongst all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

There's 15 save slots that you can use at practically any time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 features a manual save system. You can do this at practically any time, giving you the freedom to create your checkpoint in Leonida and come back to the game at a later date. Given that there are close to 100 GTA 6 Missions, this is going to come in very handy – particularly as there is no way to replay missions in GTA 6.

However, there is one big limitation. There are only 15 manual save slots in GTA 6. It would be wise to keep one at the beginning and end of each major chapter, giving you the freedom to jump around if you want or need to. As for how you save in GTA 6, you just need to follow these easy steps:

You can overwrite and load into any of these save slots in GTA 6. It's also worth mentioning that there is a single, secret 16th slot that is reserved for an auto-save which triggers after missions, if you're wasted, busted, or have some sort of major encounter in the open world.

The save system will also disable if you activate any GTA 6 cheats, forcing you to quit out of the game and reload a save that wasn't revelling in pure chaos.

#3765. From 2D to 3D and back to 2D again, the original platforming classic Super Meat Boy returns with a slick remaster complete with new levels and too many old saws

Earlier this year in a bit of a shakeup for the fleshiest kid in town, Super Meat Boy entered into a new dimension in the aptly named Super Meat Boy 3D. I've not played it but it seems like a good take on the format. Clearly, though, sometimes you just need to play the hits, as a new release of the original game is on the way in the form of Super Meat Boy Again+, a remaster with updated graphics, levels and plenty more.

What is there is very clearly Super Meat Boy, uh, again, just with a big new lick of paint. There is probably some kind of joke to be made about it being DLSS yassified, but I'm too tired to think of one, so, you get the point. But it does look pretty good! I do kind of miss the Flash game aesthetic, I think there's a real charm to the sort of visual design sensibilities you'd find from that era, but this remaster certainly ain't ugly at least. Apparently it's not just the art that's new, as there's also new music, cutscenes, secrets and "stuff."

If the animated sequences featured in the trailer, which you can have a gander at above, are included in the final game that'll be a treat to watch too, as I think they better capture the Newgrounds pseudo sub-genre of animation than the graphical overhaul. It sounds like they will be looking at the Steam page, so, a treat to look forward to while committing an act of masochism by playing it!

There's no release date attached to this remaster, so we'll all just have to sit tight for an update there. The original is still listed on Steam, but if you fancy as big a dose of nostalgia as the trailer is trying to present to you, you could always go play the original, plain old regular Meat Boy. It's playable right on Newgrounds thanks to the Flash emulator Ruffle and works like a dream! Or if you're happy to wait, you could always wishlist the new one on Steam.

#3764. Blade Runner 2099 bosses hint at a possible "triple-A" Blade Runner game in the future - just don't expect it any time soon

Blade Runner 2099 - an upcoming TV miniseries coming to Amazon Prime Video, acting as a sequel to Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner 2049 (2017) - might be getting a video game. And a 'triple-A' video game, at that. At least that's according to Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, executive producers for Blade Runner 2099 and co-CEOs of Alcon Entertainment (which owns the Blade Runner IP).

In a new interview with IGN, the duo reveal that they had thought about adapting the Blade Runner fracnhise into a game, and that - should it come to fruition - it would target "triple-A" in scope. Other than that, the duo seemed to want to keep any potential information to themselves. Given they appear to be in talks about the title, rather than in any active development, if something did come of this ideation, it would no doubt be a long, long way off. Kosove and Johnson's aim seems to be getting players to "interact" more with the world of Blade Runner, which has recently been fleshed out by the 2017 movie and is set to be developed more in the upcoming series.

Of course, we've seen Blade Runner games before. There was 1997's simply-titled Blade Runner - developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Interactive - which was a point-and-click adventure that really seemed to pick up the vibes the original Ridley Scott was putting down. An Enhanced Edition of the game was released in 2022, which is actually more of a remake than a simple enhancement.

Then, in 2023, Annapurna Interactive unveiled its very first internally-developed game, in the form of Blade Runner 2033: Labyrinth. The game, which promised to riff on the dystopian universe established in Ridley Scott's cult classic movie, would have been sandwiched squarely between that film and its sequel, Blade Runner 2049. It was going to be set in LA after the Blackout hits, but beyond that - and the fact it's coming to PC and consoles at some point - few details ever managed to break through the PR barrier before the game went dark: it's been removed from Annapurna's website and delisted from Steam. Curious.

If you want to see something more from the cyberpunk world sooner, Blade Runner 2099 releases on Prime Video on 25th November.

I'm not sure Toy Story is the best comparison here.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI has been worming its way into our everyday lives for years now, although it feels like an absolute age. If I had a nickel for everytime I heard a tech bro tell us that AI is inevitable so we should all get on board, I'd have enough money to buy back all the RAM they've taken from me. So with this in mind it's hardly surprising that yet another former game exec has come out with this exact line once again.

Ex-Take Two boss Ben Feder, who oversaw games like Red Dead Redemption and Grand Theft Auto 4, has discussed with The Game Business how one day people will accept AI—it's just a matter of time.

"When animation went from hand-drawn to computer animation, there was a massive wall of resistance," he says. "People didn’t think it looked good. Then Pixar launched Toy Story. They created a movie that not only was awesome, but used computer-generated animation and chose a subject matter that made the most of it, and did an amazing job with it.

"Once Toy Story launched, all the resistance went away. My own view is that we are one Toy Story moment away from consumer acceptance of AI in videogames in the West. In the East, they’ve already accepted it."

Feder is correct that the use of AI in game development does seem more widely accepted in countries like China and South Korea, where it's often viewed as an unremarkable part of the process. Still, for me the idea of comparing a beloved childhood film that was lovingly and painstakingly crafted with 10s of thousands of hand drawn story boards, clay models for characters, and multiple production teams, to a tool that cannot run without stolen ideas is mind-boggling.

I have some faith that machine learning can be used to help people make their jobs easier—that is, if AI companies want to make a product that's actually helpful and not one just that will make loads of money before it all comes crumbling down. But I simply cannot see how using AI for creative purposes can ever benefit a game. I think back to the current CEO of Take-Two Strauss Zelnick's view of AI: "Datasets by their very nature are backward looking, creativity by its very nature is forward looking."

#3762. Treyarch lays off lead Call of Duty writer and Zombies veteran after "approximately 20 years" of service

"Thanks to all the fans for your enthusiasm, support, and kind words over the years."

Treyarch's former Senior lead writer, Craig Houston, has been laid off after approximately 20 years of service with the developer. In a post made to both his Twitter/X account and LinkedIn, the developer thanked fans for their support during his two decades with the company and confirmed he was impacted by recent reorganistation within the studio.

"After approximately 20 years, I was sadly one of those affected by recent layoffs," he noted in his posts. "I am proud to have worked with so many talented people - many of whom will remain friends for life. Thanks to all the fans for your enthusiasm, support, and kind words over the years."

On Twitter/X, he quote tweeted a video celebrating 30 years of Treyarch and featuring footage from many of the games he worked on to share his message. It appears the layoffs referenced are part of the broad reorganistation affecting 3200 jobs that Xbox announced earlier this year. Treyarch, as part of Activision Blizzard, is owned by Xbox.

Houston is a bonafide veteran of the esteemed FPS series. His first Call of Duty title at Treyarch was Call of Duty 3, where he worked as a video editor. This was followed by World at War, Black Ops 1 through 4, where he is credited as a writer and designer. For Modern Warfare, Black Ops - Cold War, Vanguard, Modern Warfare 3, then Black Ops 6 and 7, he is listed as a member of the design team and in 'creative development'. He is not credited on this year's Modern Warfare 4.

If you've picked up a Call of Duty game in the past decade-plus, you'll have interacted with Houston's work: he was a central creative force behind the writing for Treyarch's campaign modes since 2006 (with Call of Duty 3) and the main writer for the Zombies mode since 2008 (with Call of Duty: World at War). Alongside Jimmy Zielinski, Jason Blundell, and Kevin Drew, Houston was an integral part of the evolution of the Zombies pillar of Call of Duty, and shaped it into the series-defining thing it is today. There has been a fair amount of community support for Houston since he announced the news yesterday; he was a popular dev, and a lot of the Zombies-specific fan communities online hold a lot of respect for him.

"Craig is a great guy," notes one user on Reddit. "You can tell how much he loves the story/characters he writes just by how excited he is when he talks about them in promo material."

"You're a Legend Craig, it was an honor to work with you," says ex-Treyarch vet, Tony Flame, in a reply to Houston's X post. "You created a truly special experience that will live on in the kinds of millions fans. Wishing you the best [...]."

From all of us here at Eurogamer, and myself personally - who really admires the character-work and emergent storytelling present in the Xbox 360-era Call of Duty games, specifically - we wish you the best and good luck with the future, Craig.

#3761. Congratulations to people who feel mean shooting random NPCs, because GTA 6 tries "to provide mechanisms that encourage" empathy

When you think about GTA as a series, the first thing that probably comes to mind is driving through crowds of people, gunning down whoever you like, just generally doing crime without any care in the world. I wouldn't exactly call it an empathy game, not to say that other games are any better at such a thing anyway. But with GTA 6 out, crikey, next bloody week, a new interview has gone up with co-studio head Rob Nelson where he shared that you have a bit more space to be empathetic compared to previous entries.

"Crime is a fundamental part of GTA - at least up until now, it has been," Nelson told The Guardian (via @GameRoll_, ta IGN) in a new interview. "We're trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out." When asked about whether this will be the first GTA game to encourage people to be empathetic, Nelson responded, "I would say so. I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to."

I am deeply curious as to what those mechanics may be, given that most of what we've seen so far is pretty relegated to shootin', lootin' and a bit of smoochin'. If you steal a car, is there an NPC that loses their job because of it? Can you repair the harm you caused through that action? I'm sure hardly anyone else that's vibrating through their skin in excitement for almost having the game in their fingertips will be asking such questions, I'm just often wary of empathy mechanics in games.

In any case, doesn't matter all that much for us PC lot just yet, especially because Rockstar are preparing themselves both legally and technically to tackle pirated copies of the game. Rockstar will obviously be quite busy at the moment too, not just because of that whole launching a game thing, but because UK-based workers will be voting to unionise as we speak. If formed, it could be 1600 members strong, which would make it the biggest games union in the UK. Solidarity with all the workers as the voting process continues. I hope you get the result you deserve.

GTA 6 is a wild ride – but can you replay missions once you've completed them?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Here's something that's a little surprising about Rockstar's long-awaited return to Vice City: There is no way to replay missions in GTA 6.

With over 90 main story missions in GTA 6, some of which are an absolute riot of a time while others feature pretty substantial branching paths that help shape your GTA 6 Criminal Profile system, it's no surprise that many of you are wondering how to replay your favorite moments from the campaign.

Sadly, after playing the game for over 100 hours for my GTA 6 review, I can confirm that there's simply no option to do so. It kind of makes sense when you think about it. GTA 5 did let you replay missions easy enough, but that was a way to let you back into key moments to try and complete skill challenges – Rockstar has since moved all of the GTA 6 challenges into its own spot in the progress menu. They are now far broader in scope, and primarily used to unlock GTA 6 cheats once you've wrapped up the story.

If you're worried about missing anything or wanting to play key moments from a chapter again, I would recommend that you learn the ins and outs of the GTA 6 save system – this lets you keep and load back into 15 different sessions. Otherwise, you'd have to start a whole new game just to replay a mission in GTA 6!

#3759. Cyberpunk 2077 mod Torrent adds 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City

A new Cyberpunk 2077 mod has overhauled Night City's rain, swapping the game's flat wet weather effects for individual 3D drops and adding lightning storms.

As spotted by DSOGaming, modder CyanideX's mod, Torrent, gives each raindrop its own size and falling speed. The drops also react to the player's movement, so they stream towards the windscreen when you're driving fast. If you find the wind has picked up, blustery weather can also push them sideways, too.

The rain also catches the light from street lamps, neon signs, car headlights, and taillights, and won't fall through roofs or inside buildings. Drops splash on the ground, heavy rain leaves mist in the distance, and cars throw up spray from their tyres on wet roads.

The mod complements this with a new lightning system, with branching bolts that flash and flicker before fading, and that can arrive in bursts during heavier storms.

If you like a little lightning, the frequency of bolts can be adjusted across 10 levels, and with the AudioXL mod installed, thunder follows each strike, timed to how far away it landed.

For players sensitive to flashing lights, a Reduce Flashes option dims the lightning, replaces its flicker with a single slow glow, and halves the number of strikes.

Torrent supports Nova City 2 and other weather mods, and adds extra storm effects for Nova City 2 players, including mist that rolls through the streets with the wind. It’s available now on Nexus Mods.

#3758. Rasen, out in early access now, is a PvP focused take on Dark Souls that borrows one of fighting games' best techy tricks

The idea of Dark Souls PvP has always scared me a tad. You can replace Dark Souls with Bloodborne or Elden Ring, I've typically just been a coward when it comes to the idea of fighting another, real person. They're probably going to be better than me! I don't use tactics in Souls games, I use brute force until I get my way! That being said, I do have to admit I quite like the look of Rasen, a game that is essentially just the PvP component of Dark Souls (or PvE if you just want to take on some computer-controlled enemies) that just launched into early access.

To say that it is just straight up Dark Souls combat would be unfair, from the looks of things. For one, it looks more like it leans a tad towards Sekiro with a blades-only kind of affair, whether that be big or small. And blades a plenty they have, ranging from your classic sword, to scythes, to halberds and all sorts. It's a much flashier looking affair too, with fancy slashing effects that seem to buff moves and a pace that seems much faster than Souls games tend to be.

You can take part in matches with up to eight people, which presumably extends to AI (not that kind) enemies too, in "atmospheric duels, clashes, deathmatches and more." It looks neat! And best of all, unusually for a 3D arena fighter, it has rollback netcode. For those unfamiliar, and to try and explain it simply, this is essentially a bit of tech you'll find in predominantly 2D fighting games that predicts every possible input you could make in a given moment, helping to reduce lag time and allow for tighter matches (and less rage quitting).

That's a bit harder to do in a 3D environment given that you have a lot more options at your disposal when it comes to movement, so if it works that's some impressive stuff! And we could all quite easily find out together, as a demo for Rasen is available to try out. Or, alternatively, you can just pick it up whole hog on Steam right now, as it's available in early access.

Found your GTA 6 dream car but don't want to smash its windows? Or maybe you'd rather discreetly snag a getaway vehicle without setting off an alarm. There are plenty of ways to steal a car in GTA 6, and a slim jim is one of the more civilized options.

Unlocking a car with a slim jim also lets you pop the trunk without setting off an alarm, and you might find some goodies in car trunks like weapons, drugs, or cash.

Remember that unlocking the car is only half the battle. A slim jim won't start a car with keyless ignition, but some vehicles only need to be unlocked before you can hotwire them and drive off. Keyless cars are another can of worms, requiring a key cloner.

I have no idea if this is the case of some reviewers just not being in the target audience of The Hunger Games’ latest prequel Sunrise on the Reaping or if some people who have liked the other movies found this one less moving. But looking at reviews this morning after Sunrise purple carpet photos dropped, I realized not everyone felt the way I did about the 2026 movie release.

I agree with reviews on one big point: The adaptation is faithful to Suzanne Collins’ source material, which is a pretty bleak book with a bittersweet ending in the same way the third Hunger Games book is. That’s down to several scenes I personally wanted to see play out on the big screen.

Discussing Film made a big point to call out the adaptations “faithful” take on the source material. The outlet’s Yasmine Kandil wrote:

That being said, Sunrise on the Reaping remains exceedingly faithful to the novel’s sequence of events, perhaps more so than any of its predecessors, and often down to the most minute details.

In fact, I saw that word peppered in and out of reviews. If you liked the book, you should like this movie. Or as Gizmodo's Germain Lussier more than adequately puts it, if you are a fan of this franchise, you'll dig this. It's a "love letter" to fans.

Sunrise on the Reaping, is a love letter to The Hunger Games, filled with connections, explanations, and moments designed to provide maximum delight to fans of the series. It isn’t concerned with setting up the world or reexplaining the stakes. It says, 'This is the sixth movie. If you’re watching this without context, well, that’s on you.'

Still, when it comes to SOME of these reviews, I feel like I watched a completely different movie.

At Indiewire, the grade was a C- (with a bright spot in Jesse Plemons’ performance as Plutarch), and this comment from Ryan Lattanzio is really sticking with me after perusing reviews.

Sunrise on the Reaping is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes new layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

The Guardian was equally unenthusiastic about the movie, and had seemingly a lot of fun lambasting it, calling it “overwrought” and “boring,” and even making fun of the flick’s name. ( I think Peter Bradshaw’s review highlights my earlier point, that this movie isn’t for every demographic.)

Here is yet another iteration of the utterly exhausted, unbearably extended and now surreally boring Hunger Games franchise, based on the YA bestsellers by Suzanne Collins. This one has another of the series’ convoluted faux-mythic subtitles: Sunrise on the Reaping. What, “harvest dawn” not old-timey enough?

These aren’t the only two bad reviews, they are just among the more brutal and trending. (Though it's worth pointing out plenty of outlets, like THR, Time Out and more gave the film positive reviews, and it is at the time of this writing, trending positively on review aggregators.)

Honestly, is Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping perfect? No. Mckenna Grace and Jesse Plemons are standouts, and Elle Fanning and Joseph Zada do fine jobs, but I’m not bringing up Oscars here. I also think because the movie is so long, some of the emotional deaths in the arena are blunted, and I wish we had more time with characters like Maysilee, Wiress, Beetee and Ampert.

Regardless, this movie made me feel a lot of feelings about humanity, and what humans are willing to endure. Haymitch’s story ties in so hard with Katness,’ and the end cap OG Hunger Games scene where she was able to do what he could not was both hopeful and sad at the same time. This movie emotionally wrecked me. I cried multiple times. If you are a fan of the franchise at all, you should see it on the big screen. It’s proven to be a franchise with staying power and (hopefully) more stories to tell.

#3755. Forage and fight for ingredients in a magical 1960s Italy and whip up some tasty meals Cooking Mama style in The Snackbar at the End of the World

If a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin. Outside of this whole writing about video games thing, my other lot in life is soul bound to food, so I'm always curious to see how the two can be mixed together. And earlier this week, The Snackbar at the End of the World was revealed, a wonderfully cartoonish action-adventure game set in a magical, slightly post-apocalyptic version of 1960s Italy where you go out and forage for ingredients while fending off monstrous crops before turning them into tasty meals back in your struggling restaurant.

First up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit. The whole game is hand-drawn with a colourful, comic book look that has an impressive sense of depth to it. It gives off a deep love of Italian architecture and landscapes, and that admiration clearly extends to the food too. Once you've gotten the ingredients you need, you then, loosely in the vein of Cooking Mama, prepare them and make various classic Italian dishes by performing some quick minigames. Simple, but charming! The rest of the time you're off killing some ghoulies that look like mutated fruit and veggies, with the occasional fungus-possessed hog and, uh, haunted statues? I think?

I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page. First is the content description: "This game features cartoon violence, sensitive political themes set in a fictional world, and depictions of an oppressive government committing crimes against its citizens." There is clearly a romantic quality to the game and I'd be worried if it didn't acknowledge any of the political context of the decades preceding.

The other line reads, "Every sound effect, musical note, design decision, and line of code is human-made. Because this game is about human relationships and delicious food – and that’s not a story we would ever trust AI to tell." Thank the lord! Right now there's no release date attached to The Snackbar at the End of the World, unsurprising given it was only announced this week. But while we all wait for a date, you could perhaps join me in throwing it a wishlist on Steam.

#3754. Police arrest suspect after drive-by shooting at office campus housing Xbox studio inXile

Police are still investigating the motive.

Police have arrested a suspect after a drive-by shooting at an office campus in Tustin, California, which is home to Xbox-owned studio inXile Entertainment.

According to Aftermath, officers responded to reports of a drive-by shooting at Flight at Tustin Legacy, a campus that houses inXile and other businesses, on 11th November.

"Located multiple shell casings. Nobody was hurt," Tustin Police Sergeant Christopher Peterson told the outlet. "Processed the crime scene, and then sometime [Friday] morning, a little before 11 [AM], they took a suspect into custody. And the investigation is still kind of ongoing as to where and why."

"We're relieved that no one was hurt at our inXile office," an inXile spokesperson said. "Our focus is on supporting our team, and we are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate."

Police have not given a motive, and the suspect has not been named.

InXile is the studio behind the Wasteland series, and is currently working on Clockwork Revolution.

Just because you saw GTA 6 first-person mode in the leaks doesn't necessarily mean it's in the final game

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

First-person mode for GTA 6 featured in one of the various pre-release leaks, so naturally a lot of you are wondering how to activate it now that you're taking your first steps into Leonida. It's a gorgeous world that's packed with detail, and I'm with you in wanting to get a closer look at some of the gorgeous environments.

I'm sorry to be the bearer of bad news, but there is no first-person mode in GTA 6. It's a little disappointing, given that GTA 5 received the functionality as part of the PS4/Xbox One release in 2014. Sadly, Rockstar has opted out of giving you the option to switch between first-person and third-person in GTA 6, and it's unlikely that it will come in the future.

That all being said, there are certain instances where you can look through the eyes of Jason and Lucia. If you press L2/LT to focus on a character and then click L3 and R3 you can enter first-person in GTA 6 to get a better look at specific items. You can also enter first-person mode when you pull out your phone and when you're in certain vehicles, but that's about it.

If you have modified a weapon in GTA 6 with a scope, you're also able to click R3 whilst you are aiming down sights to enter first-person mode for precision aiming. That's pretty great, all things considered, but if you were hoping to run through the GTA 6 missions in first-person, that's not going to happen.

And no, there aren't any GTA 6 cheats that will let you go into first-person either. Trust me, I checked.

Crack these vaults during a robbery to claim some cash.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 safe codes will let you unlock sealed loot containers in the main story, but also during the lucrative robbery activity, which sees you knock over gang hideouts, banks, and other cash and contraband rich institutions.

The safe codes you need in the main story or specific missions are given to you, but in order to get a safe code during a robbery (and you'll need to because they're randomised), you have two main options:

First off, you can sometimes find the code written on something inside the store or bank, like a note on a board in the back office perhaps, or maybe a guard you've incapacitated is carrying it—press L3 and R3 to activate Focus Mode and help you find it.

You can also get the code by interrogating employees. Aim your weapon at them and use the "Threaten" or "Safe Code?" prompt shown on the screen to force them to give you the information. In certain robberies, this will also force cashiers to empty the register, as in previous GTA games.

Once you have the safe code, it will appear in the lower right corner of the screen when you're interacting with the safe. You'll have to enter the four-digit code to unlock it.

Time is of the essence, so the faster you can get the code, the quicker you can open the safe and load the cash into your bag. You can tell if an establishment has a safe by selecting it on your map, which will also give you some idea of the security level (low to high) and the approximate value of the goods, so you can pick a lucrative target for your next stick up.

#3751. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

While following a peculiar trail of silver and saffron leaves around the largest roots of the Treehouse, you come across a hexagonal wooden door lying half-hidden among ivy and moss. Scraping away the dirt, you discover a faint, absurd engraving of a newspaper. What mystery is here? You turn the brass knob – strange, it is warm! – and the engraving of the newspaper flutters. The pages turn faster and faster, emitting a howling gale that bowls you head over foot. When you pick yourself up, you are inside a vast attic full of books and bricabrac, lit from one side by windows that offer no view of the outside world – just light and mist.

Tarnation! You have been lured into the eternal prison of Sunday Afternoon. Fortunately, there are several ways to escape. Each of the arcane objects before you is secretly a portal, transporting you to another site of arcane activity, in a bizarre web of diversions that cannot possibly reflect the hand of a human curator. Which will you choose?

As you step forward, your toe nudges an ornamental scroll. It growls and wriggles like a panicking caterpillar, scooting away under a table. Before you lose sight of it, you discern the title and subject of the text – it's an essay by Kyle Tam about the yokai of Promise Mascot Agency.

Deep in a drawer, you discover a sour-smelling binder full of extracts from an ancient and all but indecipherable dispute over the discovery of "generative AI" in something called "Big Walk". The stakes are long-buried, but many of the individual pieces of writing are lively. Here is Bruno Dias noting in passing that "one of the harms of the 'AI' political project is the propaganda machine dedicated to making you feel stupid and helpless." Here is a professorial interjection from Brendan Keogh calling on the warring parties to recognise when "critiques of generative AI are actually just deflected critiques of the capitalist relations of technology and labour". Here is Mike Cook arguing that "what's happening is not unusual, it's not extreme, it's not unfair and it's not a 'public flogging'." Here is a ticker tape message from Hannah Nicklin observing that "if your radical position doesn’t have room for transformation it will not be safe until it contains just you".

A footnote in the same dusty sheaf of papers points you towards another work from Mike Cook in a different drawer. This one consists of neon slides, slotted into an antique View-Master, and explores a comparison between procedural generation and street photography.

Peering at the weirdly white and opaque windowpanes, you realise there are intricate equations traced in the condensation. It appears to be a post-mortem for a "post-cosy" game called Danchi Days, in which developer Melos Han-Tani discusses wishlist conversion rates and the problem of not fitting neatly into any recognisable genre.

A snowglobe stands on a mantelpiece, the flakes still orbiting a miniature washtub as though the object had been recently shaken, even though the chamber has clearly been abandoned for decades. You put it to your ear, anticipating the faint jingle of Xmas bells. Instead, you are almost deafened by a screeching guitar chord. Here is Erin Keane to explain.

Next to the snowglobe on the mantelpiece, there's a souvenir shop conch shell, polished to a high sheen. You put that to your ear, hoping to catch the soothing shuffle of surf on shingle, and a disembodied voice tells you to piss off. Tim Sniffen has some thoughts about gentrification, and why only he should be allowed to do it.

Again, one of these mystic artefacts hides the key to your release from the suffocating stillness of Sunday Afternoon. Which will you choose? Or have you, perhaps, brought a sorcerous teleportation device of your own? Please share. Here is Joanna Newsom's Cosmia to help you think.

#3750. EA hires another former Call of Duty boss to take the lead on all Battlefield Studios' projects

EA has made some notable leadership changes within its studios group, and in who oversees the Battlefield franchise. Byron Beede, previously Battlefield's general manager, has been promoted to group general manager.

Beede announced the change on LinkedIn, saying that he now oversees EA's shooter and action-RPG portfolio, seemingly occupying the role of the late Vince Zampella.

In this stead, EA appointed Sam Cooper as Battlefield's new boss. Cooper, who also revealed his new job title on LinkedIn, previously had a stint at EA Sports, but he's mostly known for his work at Activision, where he spent the last five-ish years as Call of Duty's global product management and head of live service.

While this might seem like fairly unremarkable corporate news - executives move between rival companies all the time, after all - it reinforces a narrative that EA continues to keenly replicate Activision's Call of Duty model.

That particular push is years-old now, and it kicked off in 2021 when EA hired Byron Beede, former boss of all of Call of Duty at Activision, to lead the next evolution of Battlefield. So far, that decision has given us the very successful Battlefield 6 and its free-to-play, COD: Warzone-like battle royale mode Redsec.

To facilitate that, EA rearranged several of its studios to serve under one banner dubbed Battlefield Studios, replicating Activision's model of locking several teams around the world into developing and supporting a single game / franchise. Ripple Effect, Motive, the iconic Criterion and, of course, series creator DICE are all the Battlefield franchise's lead and support studios.

Many players argue - and I would agree - that Battlefield and Call of Duty games are more alike today than they've ever been. The user interface, the emphasis on limited-time events, the garish store cosmetics, the COD-like battle pass system - complete with a more expensive option, are all signs of that transition. And that is to say nothing of controversial changes to longstanding Battlefield tenets, such as the class system, intended to make Battlefield 6 appeal to a wider audience.

The effects of that leadership change likely won't materialise until the next Battlefield title, but it's a curious one to keep in mind as EA leans even harder into its biggest franchises following its $55bn private equity and Saudi Arabia's PIF-funded buyout.
